design_detail: Secondary analysis, by six RTI International staff, of the public-use file of the US Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) 2018 Census of Medical Examiner and Coroner Offices (CMEC), which RTI had collected for BJS by mail, web and telephone from June 2019 to March 2020, with 2018 as the reference year. 1,648 of 2,037 offices responded (80.9%): 1,341 on the long form and 307 on a shortened form of critical items. Most toxicology analyses use the 1,320 long-form offices that answered question C12i on how they provide toxicology (internally, externally, no access, not necessary); some items use up to 1,648 offices. BJS hot-deck imputations for item non-response are included. Office-level answers only: the census did not ask how many deaths were tested. Analyses are percentages, medians and chi-square tests; logistic regressions and correlation matrices are named in the methods but no results from them are shown.
can_establish: What US medical examiner and coroner offices reported in 2018 about access to toxicology testing, who decided which cases were tested, drug screening and laboratory confirmation, accreditation, forensic toxicologist staffing and salaries, specimen-retention schedules, computerized case records and participation in SUDORS and FARS, by type of toxicology access and by population served.
cannot_establish: How many deaths, or suspected overdose deaths, were tested, on which specimens or with what panel (not asked; the authors state the number is unknown); whether the offices' answers were accurate (single self-reported items, with misclassification the authors document); or how access and practice changed after 2018.

sample.recruitment: Census of all US medical examiner and coroner offices (about 2,000; 2,037 in the response-rate denominator), BJS 2018 CMEC, collected by RTI International for BJS from June 2019 to March 2020 by mail, web and telephone, with telephone follow-up for missing or doubtful answers (p. 543, Materials and methods, 1st paragraph and 2018 CMEC data collection). Public dataset obtained from the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data, ICPSR 38251 (p. 543; p. 549, Data availability).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Toxicology analyses restricted to long-form respondents who answered C12i (n = 1,320); the paper says no short-form data were used (p. 543, Measures; p. 547), yet recordkeeping and national-data items are reported for 1,647 to 1,648 offices (p. 544, Measures continued; p. 546).
sample.demographics: Offices by population served: small 550, medium 575, large 195 of 1,320. Median population served 19,186 for offices without access to toxicology and 38,719 for those with access; 154 long-form offices reported zero to four deaths (p. 544, Results, 1st paragraph). Context from the BJS report: about 80% of offices were within a coroner system (p. 544, Determination of toxicology testing need), and only 16 states have centralized offices, most offices being local, with a national median annual budget of $68,000 (p. 542, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one-time census). 389 offices did not respond; item non-response ranged from 0.0% (E1) to 5.6% (A9), handled by BJS hot-deck imputation, which the analysis keeps (p. 543).
sample.selection_effects: Respondents are offices, each answered by one person whose role is not reported. Non-responding and short-form offices are not described, and the toxicology items cover 1,320 of 2,037 offices (64.8%, editors' arithmetic). The analysts work for the organization that collected the census for BJS.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. Office characteristics come from single self-reported census items (p. 543, Measures): C12i toxicology provision (four options); A5 population served; B1 and B3 total and personnel budget; A6 and A7 accreditation; A8d and A8e forensic toxicologists and analysts or chemists on the payroll on 31 December 2018; A9d salary range; A12 and A13 ABFT certification; C14e which staff decide which cases receive toxicology (check all that apply); D9 to D11 change of testing strategy during the opioid epidemic, drug screening and laboratory confirmation; E1 and E2 computerized case management; E3b written retention schedule for toxicology specimens; F8b and F8f participation in SUDORS and FARS.

comparison.controls: Comparisons between the four toxicology-provision categories and between office sizes; the 2004 census is quoted once for computerized case management.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Differences between categories (caseload, coroner or medical examiner office, state system, rurality) are not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: The census items listed under exposure. Descriptive percentages and medians, and chi-square tests whose statistic is printed as χ without degrees of freedom (pp. 544–546); SPSS 28.0.1.1 and R 4.2.1 (p. 544, Data analysis).
outcomes.validity_norms: Unvalidated self-report. The authors document probable misclassification of C12i: of 230 offices that reported no access to or no need for toxicology, 43 later said toxicology decisions were not performed by the office, while 187 (about 14% of offices) named staff who made them; and 97 of 227 such offices answered the laboratory-confirmation question D11 (p. 548, Discussion 7th and 8th paragraphs). They also note respondents may have counted drug screens as toxicology.
outcomes.operationalization: Access to toxicology = internal or external provision on C12i. Drug screening = yes to D10 (screening at the death scene, external examination or autopsy); confirmation = yes to D11 (routine laboratory confirmation after screening) (p. 546, Table 3 notes). A forensic toxicologist is defined as performing case interpretation; an analyst or chemist does not (p. 544, Results 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; seven chi-square tests are printed and several further comparisons are described as significant or as data not shown.

analysis.effect_sizes: Toxicology provision among 1,320 offices (Table 1, p. 544): internal 78 (5.9%), external 1,012 (76.7%), no access 148 (11.2%), not needed 82 (6.2%). Access 96.4% of large and 75.1% of small offices (χ = 29.88, P < 0.001); of the 78 internal offices, 39 large, 23 medium, 16 small. Strategy changed because of the opioid epidemic 57.4% (761/1,326); drug screening 53.9% (715/1,326); routine confirmation 95.1% of screening offices (674/709) (p. 545). By category (Table 3, p. 546): changed strategy 73.1% internal, 58.2% external, 46.9% no access, 51.2% not needed (χ = 8.08, P = 0.004); screening 57.7, 55.7, 45.9, 39.5 (χ = 5.11, P = 0.024); confirmation 95.6, 96.1, 87.7, 93.8 (χ = 8.89, P = 0.003). Accreditation (Figure 1, p. 545): NAME 14.1% overall, 42.7% internal, 12.0% external, 11.6% no access, 17.5% not needed; IACME 13.4%, 14.3%, 13.1%, 16.6%, 10.0%; 73 offices (about 5.6%) accredited by both or expecting to be. Who decides which cases are tested (Figure 2, p. 545): coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall, 41.0% internal, 67.5% external; autopsy pathologist 27.0%, 60.3%, 27.5%; death investigator 24.4%, 16.7%, 25.5%. Computerized case management 44.8% (Table 4: 69.2, 49.6, 31.1, 26.8; χ = 46.61, P < 0.001); toxicology-specimen retention schedule 45.3% (79.5, 49.2, 30.4, 20.7; χ = 74.94, P < 0.001) (p. 546). SUDORS 25.3%, FARS 30.5% (p. 546). Staff: 211 full-time and 9 part-time forensic toxicologists (p. 544). Editors' calculation, treating responding offices as a sample (Wilson 95% intervals): internal 5.9% (4.8 to 7.3); no access 11.2% (9.6 to 13.0); no access or not needed 17.4% (15.5 to 19.6); screening 53.9% (51.2 to 56.6); confirmation 95.1% (93.2 to 96.4).
analysis.covariates: None. Logistic regressions and correlation matrices are named in the methods (p. 544) but no results are reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of a public dataset; no protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several results are 'data not shown' (size breakdown of internal offices, offices with few deaths, networked case systems, accreditation by both bodies, SUDORS and FARS by category); salaries in offices with external toxicology are called significantly lower with no test shown.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the internal-toxicology category has 78 offices and the salary medians rest on 58 to 62 offices.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2018, 82.6% of 1,320 responding US medical examiner and coroner offices reported access to toxicology, almost all through external laboratories; 11.2% reported no access and 6.2% no need. Small offices had access less often than large ones (75.1% against 96.4%). Coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which cases were tested. About half the offices screened for drugs at the scene, external examination or autopsy, and 95.1% of those routinely confirmed in a laboratory. Fewer than half had a specimen-retention schedule (45.3%) or a computerized case system (44.8%). The census does not record how many deaths were tested.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract matches the tables. The Discussion overstates or misstates several figures: four out of five offices with access changed their testing strategy (p. 547; Table 3 gives 73.1% internal and 58.2% external, 57.4% overall); 47% of offices had a computerized case system, 12 percentage points above the 35% of the 2004 census (p. 547; Results and Table 4 give 44.8%); NAME accreditation 14.3% (p. 547; Figure 1 gives 14.1%); overdose deaths rose 36% from 67,367 in 2018 to 105,700 in 2023 (p. 547; the rise is 56.9%, editors' arithmetic); and about 294 deaths per forensic toxicologist (p. 547), a ratio the authors themselves qualify by saying the number of suspected overdose cases that are tested is unknown (p. 548). The Conclusion that offices are adapting to the drug market rests on a single yes-or-no item about changed strategy.

timeline.event: Earlier BJS census of medical examiner and coroner offices (Hickman et al.): 35% of offices had a computerized case system (as cited, p. 547). Zaychik (2024, p. 2) cites the same census: offices serving over 250,000 people performed toxicology in drug intoxication deaths in 57% of cases, smaller offices in 34%.
Kentucky coroners' survey on the toxicology-testing mandate (cited as reference 21).
NAME position paper recommending comprehensive toxicology and autopsy in suspected overdose deaths (cited as reference 22).
BJS report on the 2018 census, Medical Examiner and Coroner Offices, 2018 (Brooks; reference 2), which this paper extends with items not published there.

Lundberg et al. (JAMA): in five states with decentralized systems, opioid laboratory tests were unavailable in about half of 74,751 injury-death investigations and in 1 in 10 unintentional overdose investigations (reference 32, as summarized, pp. 543 and 547).
This paper: toxicology capability of US offices in 2018 from the census public file.

replication.where_it_stands: The only national description of toxicology capacity in US medical examiner and coroner offices on the project's list, for 2018; no later census is reported. It describes what offices said they could do, not how many deaths were tested; death-level evidence on missing toxicology comes from studies such as Lundberg et al. (2025, as summarized here) and, for one state, from the Kentucky coroner survey (Quesinberry et al., 2019).

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Forensic Technology Center of Excellence (award 15PNIJ-21-GK-02192-MUMU), awarded by the National Institute of Justice, Office of Justice Programs, US Department of Justice; funding also provided in part by RTI International. The original 2018 CMEC data collection was performed under Cooperative Agreement 2017-MU-CX-K052 from the Bureau of Justice Statistics to RTI International (pp. 548–549, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed. The Acknowledgments state that the opinions are the authors' and do not necessarily reflect those of the US Department of Justice (p. 548).
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors are at RTI International, which collected the census for BJS; two (Smiley-McDonald, Ropero-Miller) are credited with funding acquisition (p. 548, Author contributions). Several cited works are by the same authors (references 1, 28, 29, 36, 41, 42). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount; the data are public (ICPSR 38251).

what_would_settle_it: A death-level national sample: for a representative sample of US deaths certified as, or suspected to be, drug overdoses in one year, record from case files whether toxicology was done, on which specimens and with what panel, and compare the drugs named on the certificate with those found; repeated in the next census year to measure change.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All US medical examiner and coroner offices (2,037).
1,320 offices for the main figures; the internal-toxicology category (78) and the salary medians (58 to 62 offices) are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Offices are described by toxicology provision, size and budget, but not by coroner or medical examiner type, state or caseload in the toxicology tables, and the respondent's role is unknown.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Toxicology items cover 1,320 of 2,037 offices; short-form and non-responding offices are not compared; denominators change from item to item (1,310 to 1,648) and the paper contradicts itself on whether short-form records were used.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Single self-reported items, not validated; the authors document misclassification of the key toxicology-provision item, and offices reporting no access or no need were accredited as often as or more often than those with external access (Figure 1).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One questionnaire, but three modes (mail, web, telephone), skip patterns not always followed on paper forms, and imputed values included.

Percentages reproduce from their counts, but there are no intervals, chi-square tests lack degrees of freedom, regressions named in the methods are not reported, and the Discussion contains several arithmetic errors.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: 80.9% of offices responded, but only 1,341 (65.8% of 2,037, editors' arithmetic) on the long form that carried the toxicology items; item non-response was imputed, the short-form offices were not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI prevalence checklist, because the paper describes how common practices and capacities were among US offices in one census year. Editors' summary: moderate risk of bias. The census frame and response are strong; the limits are single self-reported items with documented misclassification, toxicology items covering about two-thirds of offices, shifting denominators, and errors confined mostly to the Discussion. Citable for, as offices' own reports for 2018: toxicology provision (5.9% internal, 76.7% external, 11.2% no access, 6.2% not needed, of 1,320); access by office size (96.4% large, 75.1% small); who decides which cases are tested (coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall); drug screening (53.9%) and routine laboratory confirmation (95.1% of screening offices); NAME (14.1%) and IACME (13.4%) accreditation; specimen-retention schedules (45.3%) and computerized case systems (44.8%); SUDORS (25.3%) and FARS (30.5%) participation; and the authors' statement that the number of suspected overdose deaths tested is unknown. Not citable for: the share of deaths tested, the Discussion's 'four out of five', 47%, 36% and 294-cases-per-toxicologist figures, or any change after 2018.

key_findings.finding: The 2018 CMEC reached 1,648 of 2,037 offices (80.9%): 1,341 (81.4% of respondents) on the long form and 307 (18.6%) on a shortened form; data were collected by RTI International for BJS from June 2019 to March 2020 by mail, web and telephone, about calendar 2018.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; 2018 CMEC data collection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 1,320 offices that answered how they provide toxicology, 78 (5.9%) had an internal toxicology function, 1,012 (76.7%) used external toxicology services, 148 (11.2%) had no access to toxicology and 82 (6.2%) said they did not need it; 230 (17.4%) therefore had no access or no need.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Large offices (serving 250,000 or more; n = 195) were most likely to have access to toxicology (96.4%) and small offices (24,999 or less; n = 550) least likely (75.1%); population served was significantly related to access (χ = 29.88, P < 0.001). Of the 78 offices with internal toxicology, 39 were large, 23 medium and 16 small. Median population served was 19,186 for offices without access and 38,719 for those with access.
key_findings.locator: Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text gives 23 of 78 as 29.4% (editors' arithmetic: 29.5%). Degrees of freedom are not printed.

key_findings.finding: Responding offices reported 211 full-time and 9 part-time forensic toxicologists on staff in 2018 (data from 1,647 offices); 10% of offices employed forensic toxicologists and 7.8% forensic analysts or chemists; most offices employed no ABFT-certified staff.
key_findings.locator: Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say this undercounts toxicology professionals in external laboratories and consultants (p. 547, Discussion 3rd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Median total budgets were $1,350,000 for offices with internal toxicology, $95,878 with external services, $30,657 with no access and $20,000 for offices not needing toxicology; median minimum and maximum forensic toxicologist salaries in offices with internal toxicology were $64,024 and $112,312.
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives n = 1,320 for budgets, 834 for personnel budgets, 62 and 58 for the salary medians; the text gives n = 1,317 and n = 58.

key_findings.finding: Fewer than one in six offices were accredited by NAME or IACME: NAME 14.1% of all offices (42.7% with internal toxicology, 12.0% external, 11.6% no access, 17.5% not needed) and IACME 13.4% (14.3%, 13.1%, 16.6%, 10.0%); 73 offices (about 5.6%) were accredited by both or expected to be by the end of 2018.
key_findings.note: Figure values are printed data labels in the image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; not in the text layer). The Discussion gives NAME 14.3% (p. 547).

key_findings.finding: Coroners were most often responsible for deciding which cases received toxicology (64.7%, check all that apply, n = 1,340); by Figure 2, coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall, 41.0% in offices with internal toxicology and 67.5% with external; autopsy pathologist 27.0%, 60.3% and 27.5%; death investigator 24.4%, 16.7% and 25.5%. About 80% of offices were within a coroner system according to the BJS report.
key_findings.locator: Results, Determination of toxicology testing need (p. 544); Figure 2 (p. 545)
key_findings.note: Figure 2 values are printed data labels in the image (read on a 300-dpi rendering). The 'Total' bars are not the weighted average of the two groups shown (editors' arithmetic), and n = 1,340 exceeds the 1,320 who answered C12i.

key_findings.finding: 57.4% (761 of 1,326) of offices said their toxicology testing strategy changed because of the rise in drug-related deaths and the opioid epidemic; 53.9% (715 of 1,326) performed drug screening tests at the death scene, external examination or autopsy; 95.1% (674 of 709) of those routinely confirmed screens with laboratory toxicology. By category (Table 3): changed strategy 73.1%, 58.2%, 46.9% and 51.2%; screening 57.7%, 55.7%, 45.9% and 39.5%; confirmation 95.6%, 96.1%, 87.7% and 93.8% (internal, external, no access, not needed).
key_findings.locator: Results, Forensic toxicology testing strategy (p. 545); Table 3 (p. 546)
key_findings.note: Offices with access were more likely to change strategy (χ = 8.08, P = 0.004), to screen (χ = 5.11, P = 0.024) and to confirm (χ = 8.89, P = 0.003).

key_findings.finding: 44.8% of offices had a computerized case management system and 45.3% a retention schedule for toxicology specimens (n = 1,648); by category, 69.2% and 79.5% with internal toxicology, 49.6% and 49.2% external, 31.1% and 30.4% no access, 26.8% and 20.7% not needed (χ = 46.61 and 74.94, both P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results, Recordkeeping and evidence retention practices, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Participation in national drug data collections was low: 25.3% of offices took part in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS; n = 1,647) and 30.5% in NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS; n = 1,648). The text gives 20.8% (SUDORS) and 26.9% (FARS) for offices with external toxicology and 2% or less for each other category.
key_findings.locator: Results, MEC participation in drug-related national data collections
key_findings.note: The category figures cannot be shares within each category: if they were, overall participation among the 1,320 could not exceed about 16% (SUDORS) and 21% (FARS) (editors' arithmetic); they are probably shares of all 1,320 offices.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the annual number of suspected overdose cases that receive toxicology testing is unknown, even in offices with in-house testing, and that data from at least two states indicate testing is not done at the level needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins p. 547, right column; statement on p. 548)

key_findings.finding: The authors' context figure: dividing 67,367 drug overdose deaths in 2018 by the toxicologist count gives about 294 cases for each forensic toxicologist to interpret within the death investigation system.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 67,367/220 (the paper's 211 full-time plus 9 part-time) = 306; 67,367/230 (the BJS count quoted in the same paragraph) = 293. The ratio assumes all overdose deaths are interpreted by toxicologists employed by offices, whereas most offices use external laboratories.

key_findings.finding: Second-hand, from a study of five states with decentralized systems: opioid laboratory tests were unavailable in about half of injury-death investigations (51% of 74,751 in the Discussion) and in 1 in 10 unintentional overdose death investigations.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 542, continues p. 543); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 547)
key_findings.note: As summarized from reference 32 (Lundberg et al., JAMA 2025); the Discussion calls it a 2021 CDC study, which is its data year.

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors give: the census was voluntary, with 63 questions of which 8 were specific to toxicology; respondents did not always answer every question and skip patterns on paper forms were not always followed; the toxicology-provision question depended on respondents' interpretation (some may have counted drug screens), and answers to later questions suggest misclassification for about 14% of offices.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample definitions conflict: the paper says no short-form data were used (pp. 543, 547), but refers to 'the full 1648 long form sample' and to 1,647 offices answering A8d 'on the CMEC long form' (p. 544), while the long form had 1,341 respondents (p. 543); the response-rate denominator is 2,037 on p. 543 and 2,036 on p. 547.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which offices enter the 1,647 to 1,648 totals (staff counts, computerized systems, retention schedules, SUDORS and FARS); they appear to include short-form or imputed records.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says four out of five offices with access to toxicology changed their testing strategy, but Table 3 gives 73.1% (internal) and 58.2% (external), and 57.4% overall.

The Discussion gives 47% of offices with a computerized case system, 12 percentage points above the 35% of the 2004 census, against 44.8% in the abstract, Results and Table 4; NAME accreditation 14.3% against 14.1% in Figure 1; and it calls the 73 offices accredited by both bodies 5.6% 'of these accredited' offices, whereas the Results give them as about 5.6% of all offices.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Results values; the 2004 comparison is about 10 points, not 12 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Context arithmetic: overdose deaths are said to have risen 36% from 67,367 in 2018 to 105,700 in 2023 (p. 547) and by an additional 35% after 2018 (p. 542); from 67,367 to 105,700 is a 56.9% rise (36.3% is the rise divided by the 2023 figure), and from 70,630 in 2019 it is 49.7% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: These trend percentages should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The SUDORS and FARS figures for offices with external toxicology (20.8%, 26.9%) and for the other categories (2% or less) are worded as shares within each category but are incompatible with overall participation of 25.3% and 30.5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Participation by toxicology category cannot be cited; only the overall figures are usable.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's 'Total' bars (pathologist 27.0%, coroner 64.7%, investigator 24.4%) are not the weighted averages of the internal and external groups (about 29.8%, 65.6% and 24.9%, editors' arithmetic), and the stated n = 1,340 exceeds the 1,320 offices that answered the toxicology-provision question, although the text says only offices requesting toxicology are shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of the overall 64.7% is uncertain; it is close enough to the group figures to be cited as 'about two-thirds' with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods name logistic regressions and correlation matrices, but none is reported; chi-square statistics are printed as χ without degrees of freedom; external-toxicology offices are said to pay significantly lower salaries with no test shown; the Discussion's 'about 300' offices with five or fewer deaths a year does not match the Results' 154 offices with zero to four deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the descriptive percentages and the seven printed chi-square tests can be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Offices reporting no access to toxicology were accredited by IACME more often (16.6%) than offices with external access (13.1%), and offices reporting no need were accredited by NAME more often (17.5%) than offices with external access (12.0%) (Figure 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: An unexpected pattern that fits the misclassification of the toxicology-provision item the authors describe; category comparisons should be cited with that caveat.
